SeriesLinearAlgAccessor::cholesky¶

Back to SeriesLinearAlgAccessor API Reference

Signatures¶

Series SeriesLinearAlgAccessor::cholesky(bool upper = false) const
Series SeriesLinearAlgProxy::cholesky(bool upper = false) const

What It Does¶

cholesky() factors each symmetric positive-definite matrix into one triangular factor. With the default lower form it returns L such that A = L L^T. With upper=true it returns U such that A = U^T U.

Factoring Positive Energy¶

A positive-definite matrix assigns strictly positive quadratic energy x^T A x to every nonzero vector. Cholesky turns that coupled energy into a triangular coordinate transform. The factor is unique when its diagonal is positive, making it a particularly efficient foundation for solves and inverses involving covariance and normal-equation matrices.

Parameter¶

upper (bool, default false) Return the upper factor when true; otherwise return the lower factor. This changes which triangle contains meaningful values, not the shape.

Shape Contract¶

Input [...,n,n] produces [...,n,n]. The last two dimensions must be square; every leading batch item is factored independently.

Gradient¶

Reverse mode differentiates the factorization identity and returns a symmetric sensitivity for the original matrix. The input must remain positive definite; the derivative becomes poorly conditioned as an eigenvalue approaches zero.

Examples¶

Example 1. Reconstruct the matrix from the default lower factor.

auto a = pluss::make_series({{4.0, 2.0}, {2.0, 3.0}});
auto l = a.linearalg.cholesky();
std::cout << l << "\n";
std::cout << l.linearalg.mm(l.transpose(0, 1)) << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[2, 0],
  [1, 1.4142136]]
pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[4, 2],
  [2, 3]]

Example 2. upper=true returns the transposed orientation.

auto a = pluss::make_series({{4.0, 2.0}, {2.0, 3.0}});
std::cout << a.linearalg.cholesky(true) << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[2, 1],
  [0, 1.4142136]]

Example 3. A non-positive-definite matrix is rejected rather than producing an invalid factor.

try {
  std::cout << pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {2.0, 1.0}}).linearalg.cholesky();
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::cout << e.what() << "\n";
}

Output¶

subsp::math::linalg::cholesky: matrix is not SPD

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Symmetry alone is insufficient; every eigenvalue must be strictly positive.

  • Only the selected triangle represents the factor; the opposite triangle is zero.

  • Near-singular positive-definite matrices can yield unstable factors and gradients.

Summary¶

cholesky() converts an SPD matrix into a lower or upper triangular factor, preserving batches and supporting reverse mode.

See Also¶

  • cholesky_solve: solve from an existing factor.

  • cholesky_inverse: invert from an existing factor.
